item.title: Scotch at the docks tests India-UK trade arrangement's tariff concessions
item.description: The India-UK trade pact offers lower duties on eligible Scotch whisky imports, but the applicable tariff depends on the classification of goods under the Customs Tariff and exemption notification ...
item.dc:creator: TNC Rajagopalan
item.content:encoded: Last week, Reuters reported that several consignments of Scotch whisky imported from the United Kingdom (UK) were held up at the ports. The importers seek clearance at 75 per cent Customs duty under the India-UK trade agreement, whereas the Customs seek duty at 150 per cent. On Friday, the Commerce Secretary said that the Ministry of Finance had engaged with the stakeholders and that India would honour the duty concessions under the agreement.

item.title: India invites Singapore universities to set up campuses, build townships
item.description: India has sought Singapore's expertise in developing university townships modelled on NUS's University Town, alongside deeper cooperation in education, research and innovation ...
item.dc:creator: Auhona Mukherjee
item.content:encoded: India has invited Singaporean universities to establish campuses in the country and sought Singapore's expertise in developing its proposed university townships, drawing on the National University of Singapore's (NUS) University Town model, Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi said on Sunday. The proposals were discussed during Joshi's bilateral meeting with Singapore's Education Minister Desmond Lee at Singapore Management University (SMU), following the inauguration of the fourth Singapore-India Hackathon. In a post on X, Joshi said the two sides discussed strengthening cooperation across school education, higher education, skilling, research and innovation. “I invited more Singaporean universities to establish campuses in India and sought Singapore’s expertise in developing our proposed University Townships, drawing from the NUS University Town model,” Joshi said in his post. The invitation comes amid India's efforts to attract foreign universities under the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020. In 2022, the UGC had identified Singapore's leading institutions, including NUS, Nanyang Technological University (NTU) and Singapore Management University (SMU), among around 260 foreign universities shortlisted as potential partners for collaboration and campus expansion in India. Former UGC chairman M Jagadesh Kumar had said the commission would work with interested Singaporean institutions to facilitate their entry into India. However, none of the Singaporean universities features on the UGC's current list of foreign higher education institutions with campuses in India. Under the UGC's 2023 regulations, foreign universities can establish campuses in India, subject to eligibility and regulatory approvals. As of August 2026, the UGC had issued 16 letters of intent to 15 foreign institutions from Australia, Italy, the UK and the US. India's proposed university townships, meanwhile, were announced in the Union Budget 2026-27, which envisaged five such integrated academic zones near major industrial and logistics corridors. These are expected to bring together multiple universities, colleges, research institutions, skill centres and residential facilities. The Ministry of Education has initiated consultations with state governments, academic institutions and industry representatives to develop the framework. NUS's University Town is an integrated campus ecosystem that combines residential facilities, teaching infrastructure, study clusters and common spaces to encourage academic and social engagement. The two ministers also discussed mutual recognition of qualifications, deeper teacher and student exchanges, joint capacity-building programmes and stronger industry-academia linkages. “We also discussed collaboration in AI in education, advanced materials, clean energy, fintech, semiconductors and other emerging technologies, alongside joint research and support for deep-tech start-ups and innovators through Bharat Innovates,” Joshi said. Joshi also proposed hosting the fifth India-Singapore Hackathon in India in 2027 and establishing a periodic India-Singapore Higher Education Institutions Conference. The fourth edition of the hackathon, organised by SMU's Institute for Innovation and Entrepreneurship, the All India Council for Technical Education and the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell, is being held in Singapore from November 15 to 17, bringing together around 120 students from the two countries.

item.title: Noel Tata questions big investments as $185 billion group feud deepens
item.description: Noel Tata has backed investments in strategic sectors but questioned whether projects are being executed with enough discipline ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Shinjini Datta Noel Tata, chairman of the trusts that control Tata Group, questioned whether some of the conglomerate’s biggest investments are being executed with enough discipline, deepening a dispute over capital allocation, control and a potential listing of its holding company. The clash has widened as the group commits billions of dollars to semiconductors, aviation, electronics and electric-vehicle batteries, while the trusts that own 66% of Tata Sons Pvt. resist a listing that would bring outside shareholders into the closely held parent. The dispute now reaches beyond succession and ownership to how a group generating about $185 billion in annual revenue is funded, governed and run. “The question is, do we have the discipline when we execute projects, and not the direction?” Tata said Saturday at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi. “How will projects with a long gestation period succeed if we don’t have discipline?” Much of the expansion has been pursued under Natarajan Chandrasekaran, the professional executive who has led Tata Sons since 2017. A confidential analysis prepared by Tata Trusts and reviewed by Bloomberg News estimated that semiconductors, electronics and aviation would require more than 2 trillion rupees ($21 billion) in additional capital. The governance dispute widened after Tata Sons’ board backed Chandrasekaran for another five-year term on Sept. 17 despite Noel Tata’s opposition. A spokesperson for Tata Sons didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on his remarks about execution, capital allocation and a possible listing, sent over the weekend. Tata companies generated about $185 billion in revenue in the year through March and own businesses ranging from Jaguar Land Rover to Tetley tea. Tata Trusts owns 66% of Tata Sons, and profits from group companies ultimately help fund philanthropy. That ownership structure has also allowed Tata Sons to support businesses through periods of weak returns or heavy investment. Noel Tata has argued that a public listing, and the arrival of thousands of outside shareholders, could make that model harder to sustain. “My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way,” he said. With 30,000 to 40,000 shareholders, “profit may take precedence over philanthropy.” Pressure to go public intensified after the Reserve Bank of India classified Tata Sons as an upper-layer non-banking financial company, a designation that carries listing requirements. The Trusts have opposed that outcome and explored a restructuring aimed at keeping the parent private. Noel Tata said the Trusts remain “100% behind” investments in projects of national importance, even as he called for greater discipline in how the group executes them and allocates capital.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / What travellers need to know about US flights after nationwide ground stop

What travellers need to know about US flights after nationwide ground stop The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 pm ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from US airports

Travelers sit on a baggage carousel during a nationwide ground stop at LaGuardia Airport (LGA) in the Queens borough of New York, US, on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. A nationwide ground stop was canceled by the Federal Aviation Administr | Image: Bloomberg

AP Washington 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 11:15 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Officials assured passengers that the US airspace was safe and operational after a nationwide ground stop that was initiated out of caution caused massive travel disruptions. The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 pm ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from US airports. Of the 41,000 flights scheduled Saturday, more than 6,400 had been canceled by Saturday night, according to FlightAware. More than 800 flights scheduled for Sunday were cancelled, it said. But officials said the air traffic control system was operational and expected airline schedules to fully recover by the end of Sunday, smoothing out ahead of the Thanksgiving travel rush.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack and no lives were at risk. Also Read

Flights halted at airports across US due to ATC communications problems

Here's what to know: Flights have resumed but disruption continues Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said the system was stable Saturday. Several thousand flights were able to fly after the ground stop, but ultimately, some 12,000 scheduled flights were unable to take off Friday, he said. Officials acknowledged the disruption but said safety was paramount. Bedford offered an apology for stranded travelers and thanked air traffic controllers, pilots and flight attendants for managing the fallout. He said officials were confident the system is operating safely or else they would keep airplanes on the ground.

Airlines remove change fees for affected passengers Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight or a full refund if a flight is cancelled. Bedford said the administration was working closely with airlines and said they were waiving all terms and conditions. Some airlines were allowing passengers to rebook if they had travel scheduled Friday or Saturday. Others extended the offer to people with reservations for Sunday or even Monday. Bedford advised passengers to contact their airlines. The system was overloaded while part of it was being upgraded A contractor was replacing a section of the system's old and discontinued copper wire with new fiber wire in a remote location Friday afternoon, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Saturday. That kind of work has been happening across the country and across industries for decades, he said.

But on Friday, the router in that location started overloading the air traffic control system and causing intermittent disruptions to communications and radar feeds. When officials couldn't quickly locate the cause of the overload, they grounded flights nationwide. "We did that out of an abundance of caution," Bedford said. "I'm sorry that we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons."   Officials stressed that the ground stop was not the result of a system outage or nefarious activity by a foreign actor. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was the cause. The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved USD 12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work. About 70 per cent of copper wire has been switched to fiber already, officials said Saturday.

The Microsoft outage was unrelated to the stoppage Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after its own massive outage. There was no indication the FAA ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Microsoft services offline Thursday, according to federal officials and a company spokesperson. Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Users reported Microsoft 365 services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were interrupted.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
